title: LLM trading bot?
author: RedStar1996
selftext:
LLMs are getting better with each model released. They will never be truly deterministic (or it will take some time to get that) but they will improve their consistency. I know that is probably a major obstacle in LLM trading.

I was just wondering if this is an area that people are getting into recently. I don’t mean using an LLM to create systematic trading rules or regular ML models.

I’m talking about teaching an LLM your rules and then having it make the decisions and trade for you. In someway, it would be a combination between discretionary and systematic trading, but fully automated.

I haven’t been able to find a lot of discussion on this topic. Does anyone have opinions on this? Is this even feasible? Is there an obvious reason why this isn’t a good path?

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
I've looked into this a fair bit, and for 30s-3min holds I think there are three obvious reasons it's a tough path:

1. latency. an LLM call takes anywhere from under a second to several seconds, and it varies. on a 30-second trade that's a big chunk of the move gone before you even send the order, and the delay is worst exactly when the market is moving fast.

2. you can't really backtest it. the model has very likely seen the price history you'd test on, so a backtest leaks the future without you noticing. forward results are the only honest test, and at this horizon you need hundreds of trades before they mean anything.

3. drift. people who ran LLMs as the decision layer for months report it slowly stops following the rules, a bit more "creative" each week. on top of that, the same input can give different answers. if the rules are clear enough to teach an LLM, they're usually clear enough to just code, and code is fast, cheap and does the same thing every time.

where LLMs do help: writing and checking the code, reading news or filings at slower horizons, journaling and reviewing your trades. a few people here (myself included) found the same thing: AI in research, plain code in execution.

the academic side agrees too. when LLM trading agents were re-tested over long periods with survivorship and lookahead removed, most of the claimed edge disappeared.

comments.author: k1_r1
comments.body:
for 30 second holds id flip it around. have the llm read your rules once and write them as actual code, then run the code. same inputs give the same trade every time, you can backtest it, and when it does something dumb you can see which line did it. with the llm making every call live you cant really backtest at all, rerun the same day and it might trade differently

where ive seen llms help intraday is as a filter on top, like flagging news days to sit out. the code still decides the trades

i work on portfoliolab which does the plain english rules to code to backtest part. its built more for daily and swing stuff than 30 second futures though, so for your timeframe youd port the logic to whatever your broker runs

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: at 30 second to 3 minute holds the clock kills it before the determinism does. a call to a good model takes a few seconds, sometimes ten, so by the time it decides a real chunk of your hold is gone. testing is the other wall: the model has read the news about every day you'd backtest on, so a replay on past data flatters it. I'd only trust it run forward on paper.

comments.author: fomoz
comments.body: You can run your own LLM trading bots on my platform, for free, forever. But not for holding times that are that short, the cadence I usually use is checking the market every minute and one decision takes around 10 to 30s depending on the model. So they day trade/swing trade.

comments.author: Technical-Athlete-9
comments.body:
Ernest Chan wrote a recent book called something like “Generative AI for Trading and Investment Management.” It covered everything I use it for and gave me a couple new ideas. Check that out. Ernie knows what he’s talking about.

Short timeframe futures trading isn’t one of the topics IIRC.
